hook: The British scientist who invented the World Wide Web, and gave it away.

pages.x: Tim Berners-Lee was born in London in 1955. Both his parents worked on one of the first computers sold to businesses, the Ferranti Mark 1.

pages.t: A computer from an old TV
pages.x: At Oxford he built his own computer out of an old television, a soldering iron and spare parts. He was banned from the university's computer after he and a friend were caught hacking into it.

In 1989, at CERN, the physics laboratory near Geneva, he proposed a way to link documents on different computers. His boss wrote "vague but exciting" on the proposal. By 1990 he had written the first web browser and server.
pages.fx: The web made the internet easy for everyone. Billions of people now use it every day to learn, work, shop and talk.

pages.x: The first website went online in 1991 and explained what the web was. It ran on a computer in his office with a handwritten label warning people not to turn it off.
In 1993 CERN agreed to let anyone use the web for free, with no patents and no fees. He never became rich from it.
In 1994 he founded the World Wide Web Consortium, which sets the rules that make web pages work everywhere.
At the opening of the London Olympics in 2012, he sat at a computer in the stadium and typed a message that lit up around the crowd: "This is for everyone."
He was knighted in 2004, and in 2016 won the Turing Award, the highest prize in computing. He now campaigns for people to control their own data online.
Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web and gave it away for free, changing how humanity shares knowledge.
